Doctors drew blood repeatedly, the needles glinting under fluorescent lights as nurses adjusted the dripping fluids. When his condition worsened, he required another procedure to clear his airway. She stood watching the medical equipment roll past, feeling utterly powerless. The care had been fragmented; specialists changed shifts without thorough handoffs, and when the family raised concerns about the delay in his stabilization, they were met with clipped responses and closed doors. She had come to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it. She also believed that the people or institutions that should have protected her let them down. She kept replaying the hours he lay unresponsive, certain that she should have protected others and that she had failed. In the months that followed, these appraisals settled alongside a constellation of experiences that occupied her days. She was unable to relax even when she knew she was in a safe place, her shoulders perpetually drawn tight. Her eyes constantly scanned the surroundings for signs of danger, tracking every passing car or distant siren. When a loud truck backfired outside her home, her chest tightened and her hands trembled, a strong physical reaction when something reminded her of the stressful experience. She tried to erase the memory of the event, changing her daily routes, discarding old hospital paperwork, and refusing to look at photographs from that period. She avoided anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, staying meticulously occupied at her grocery shop to prevent any emotional surge. When she tried to deliberately recall what happened, she found it difficult to access the memory; the facts remained known, but she was unable to find words to describe it. Instead, she would be caught off guard by a full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, leaving her breathless and disoriented. She kept asking others to reassure her that she was okay, asking her husband repeatedly to confirm that she was alright, that she was not broken, that they were safe. Each reassurance helped only until the next morning, when the tension returned. Now, at her dry goods shop in a quiet commercial strip, these habits had become her daily reality. When a regular customer sliced his palm on a cardboard box, the sight of the blood made her stomach lurch and her shoulders lock. She stepped back behind the counter, her pulse hammering, and forced herself to call a first-aid kit without looking directly at the wound. The last time she tried to schedule her annual physical, the thought of undergoing a medical examination or procedure unraveled her completely; she cancelled the appointment and has not booked another since. Her husband noticed how she flinches at his bandages, how they avoid discussing the hospital visit altogether, and how their conversations have narrowed to logistics to keep any feeling at bay. The shop's steady rhythm has become her anchor, yet she watches the front door every time the bell chimes, certain that another crisis could arrive at any moment. She finally came to therapy because the silence inside her shop had grown louder than the fear, and because she could no longer carry the weight of a system she believed had failed them alone. What she hopes for is simply to stop bracing for a blow that has already fallen, and what frightened her most was that the dread might never let go.

Vignette: Mae

Mae is a 57-year-old married woman of Thai descent who has run a small fabric and sewing notions shop in the same neighborhood for nearly twenty years. She is soft-spoken and precise in the way she describes things - the kind of person who folds cloth along exactly the right grain before she cuts it. That same precision, she says, is what makes it so hard when her mind refuses to stay where she puts it.

Eight years ago, Mae's youngest son, Decha, then fourteen, collapsed at school during a physical education class. What followed was three weeks in a pediatric intensive care unit, a diagnosis of viral myocarditis, two episodes where physicians told Mae and her husband that Decha might not survive the night, and an emergency transfer to a larger hospital two hours from their home. Mae slept in waiting rooms. She watched nurses move quickly and quietly around her son's bed in ways that told her more than any doctor's words. She remembers the particular sound of the cardiac monitor - a steady, ordinary beep that she learned to listen to with her whole body, terrified of any change. Decha survived. He is now a healthy young man in university. Mae knows this. She reminds herself of it often. It does not always help.

In the years since, Mae has rebuilt most of the surface of her life. The shop opens at nine. She orders inventory, advises customers on thread weight and interfacing, teaches a small alterations class on Thursday evenings. Her husband notices that she seems fine. She mostly is, in the way that a person can be fine while carrying something heavy in both hands.

What Mae does not tell many people is that she still cannot hear a certain kind of alarm - a medical alert tone, the beep of a truck reversing, even the timer on her shop's back-room microwave - without her chest tightening and her hands going cold. She has replaced the microwave timer with a silent visual model. She does not fully understand why she did this until she tries to explain it here.

She avoids the hospital where Decha was first admitted. This means she has not visited a neighbor who was recently treated there, something that troubles her conscience. She tells herself she is busy with the shop. She knows that is not the whole truth.

Sleep is where the past finds her most reliably. She wakes between two and four in the morning, sometimes from a dream in which she is standing outside a glass door she cannot open, watching a monitor she cannot read. Other times she simply wakes, already frightened, without knowing why. She lies still so as not to disturb her husband, running through a mental inventory of everyone she loves, checking that they are accounted for. She has become, she says with a small, self-aware laugh, "a woman who needs to know where everyone is."

When Decha calls home less frequently during exam periods, Mae finds herself constructing quiet catastrophes. She will send a casual message and wait for the reply with a vigilance she recognizes as disproportionate but cannot quite release. She describes this as feeling like standing at the edge of something, always. She is not depressed, she is careful to say. She loves her life. She loves her shop, her husband, her son. It is more that the world has shown her, once, in vivid and undeniable detail, exactly how quickly everything can change, and she has not entirely found her way back from that knowledge.

She came to therapy, she explains, because Decha recently had a routine cardiac follow-up appointment, and for the two weeks beforehand Mae could not eat a full meal. She sat behind the shop counter and cut fabric and smiled at customers and felt, the entire time, as though she were still in that waiting room - still listening, still watching the door.

Rangi Taufa is a 71-year-old Tongan-American man who has been married for over forty years and works part-time as a cashier at a grocery store in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. He came to the clinic several months after the event that changed him, referred by his primary care physician who had grown concerned about his withdrawn affect and persistent sleep difficulties. He sat quietly in the intake session, hands folded in his lap, and spoke in careful, measured sentences - until he couldn't.

Approximately eight months ago, Rangi was present at a community gathering held in the fellowship hall of his church when a violent altercation broke out between two men near the entrance. One of the men produced a weapon. What followed lasted perhaps two minutes, though Rangi cannot account for the sequence with any confidence. A young mother who had been standing near the doorway was struck. Her infant, who had been in her arms, began to cry - a sound that cut through the noise of the hall in a way Rangi describes as impossible to unhear. He was close enough to see everything and far enough to be unable to intervene. By the time the situation was contained, the woman had sustained serious injuries. The men responsible were removed from the scene, but in the months that followed, no formal charges were pursued. The church leadership, where Rangi had worshipped for over twenty years, declined to discuss the matter publicly and made no formal acknowledgment to those who had witnessed it. Rangi was never contacted by anyone in an official capacity.

In the weeks that followed, something shifted in him that he struggled to name. He had come to feel, with a quiet but absolute certainty, that the institution he had trusted most had simply closed its doors on what happened - and on him. He did not speak of this readily, but it sat in him like a stone. He had also come to believe, though he found it difficult to articulate, that the people responsible had simply moved on while he remained anchored to a moment he could not fully reconstruct. When he tried to explain what had happened - to his wife, to his doctor, to the intake clinician - he would begin and then lose the thread entirely, sometimes mid-sentence, sometimes before he had even reached the moment of violence itself. He described the memory as a collection of fragments with gaps between them, like a photograph torn into pieces and reassembled with pieces missing. He could not tell a coherent story of the event even to himself, and this disturbed him in ways he did not fully understand.

At the grocery store where he works three shifts a week, Rangi stands behind his register near the main entrance. The automatic doors open and slam throughout his shift - a sound that, on certain days, sends a jolt through his body before he has had time to think. He has developed a habit of watching customers as they approach his lane, tracking their hands, their posture, the direction of their gaze, alert for something he cannot quite name but is certain he would recognize if it appeared. Shoppers with infants in carts present a particular difficulty; the sound of a crying baby - even a brief, ordinary cry - can stop him mid-transaction. He has twice needed to ask a colleague to cover his register, offering no explanation.

At home, Rangi describes feeling, much of the time, as though he is observing his own life from a distance. He participates in family dinners, accompanies his wife to appointments, tends his small garden - but reports feeling little of what he used to feel doing these things. He used the phrase "dead inside" without apparent distress, as though he had already made a kind of peace with it, or perhaps simply run out of language to protest it.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife. She told him, gently but plainly, that she felt she had lost him. He did not disagree with her. What he hopes for, he said at the end of the intake session, is simply to understand what happened - to be able to hold the story of that night in a way that makes some kind of sense. What he fears is that he never will.

At 22, Amir should be reveling in the possibilities of young adulthood-his burgeoning career as a UX designer, evenings spent with friends, and dreams of travel. Instead, he navigates each day as though swimming through a thick fog, where moments of clarity are fleeting and often engulfed by memories of the catastrophic flood that altered his life just over a year ago.

The disaster struck on a rainy Thursday, the type of day that often brought him solace as he huddled in his workspace at the tech startup. He recalls how the office buzzed with energy, the rhythmic tapping of keyboards punctuating the air. But when the skies unleashed their fury, those familiar sounds were drowned out by the rising water. He remembers his heartbeat quickening as he received frantic messages from friends and family, urging him to leave. The images of water pouring into his office, submerging desks and computers, remain etched in his mind. Amir can almost feel the cold, rushing water lapping at his ankles, the panic that surged as he realized he was trapped.

In the days following, Amir becomes the reluctant hero. He joins rescue teams, helping to evacuate neighbors and friends. He wades through the muddy streets, pulling people from their homes, listening to the cries of children and the desperate calls of the elderly. Each rescue is a mix of adrenaline and dread, but Amir pushes through, driven by a sense of duty. In those moments, he feels alive, as if he can escape his own fear. Yet, he cannot shake the weight of loss-the homes destroyed, the lives uprooted, and the silence that follows the chaos.

As weeks turn into months, Amir tries to return to a semblance of normalcy. He immerses himself in work, brainstorming user experiences for a new app that promises to connect communities in crisis. He pours over design mockups, but his mind wanders. The floodwaters rise unbidden in his thoughts, and he finds himself fixating on the faces of those he couldn't save. He often catches himself staring blankly at his screen, fingers hovering over the keyboard, while vivid memories of that day replay in his mind. It's as if he's watching a movie-his own movie-where he is both the hero and the spectator, unable to change the ending.

Amir's social life crumbles. Friends invite him out, but he declines, feeling that he has nothing to offer. The laughter and joy of others feel like a distant echo, a reminder of a life he no longer recognizes. He spends hours in his small apartment, the walls closing in, the silence only broken by the sound of rain pattering against the window. On particularly stormy nights, he finds himself paralyzed with anxiety, heart racing as thunder rolls. He thinks he hears the water rising again, the panic creeping back, forcing him to relive the terror. 

He avoids places that remind him of the flood-the local park once filled with laughter, now a reminder of the treacherous waters. He stops going to the coffee shop down the street where he used to meet friends, the barista's cheerful greetings now a bitter contrast to his internal turmoil. Amir feels trapped in his own mind, a prisoner of the memories that replay with relentless clarity. 

Despite the turmoil, there's a flicker of hope. Amir seeks solace in sketching. He finds peace in the lines and curves of design, a world he can control. He sketches user interfaces that feel like a refuge from his reality, allowing his creative flow to drown out the chaos. The designs become a form of therapy, a way to express the emotions he cannot voice. 

As he navigates this delicate balance of work and memory, Amir understands he is in a battle against an invisible foe. Each day brings fresh challenges; moments of clarity often overshadowed by waves of anxiety. He clings to the hope that, through his art and the support of those who still reach out, he might someday find a way back to that vibrant life he once took for granted. For now, he takes it one day at a time, the echoes of the past ever-present, yet he knows he is not alone in his journey.

Amir sits in the therapy room, fingers drumming softly against their knees, a habit that has become a small comfort in the wake of the chaos that has enveloped their life. At 26, they are a veterinarian, a profession that has always brought them joy and fulfillment. Amir loves the sounds of animals in their clinic-the soft mews of kittens, the gentle barks of dogs, the thumping tails that wag in excitement. But lately, those sounds feel distant, overshadowed by a haunting memory that replays in their mind.

The mugging happened on a Tuesday evening. Amir had just finished a long shift at the clinic, where they had treated a stray dog with a broken leg. As they walked to their car, the sun began to dip below the horizon, casting long shadows on the pavement. It was a route they had taken countless times, a routine as familiar as the back of their hand. But that evening, the air felt different-charged, almost electric. 

As Amir approached their vehicle, they noticed someone lingering near the parked cars. A shiver ran down their spine, but they brushed it off, convincing themselves it was just their imagination. As they fumbled with their keys, they felt a presence behind them. Before they could turn, a hand gripped their shoulder, spinning them around. The assailant's face was masked, eyes cold and unyielding. The world around them blurred as fear gripped their heart; they remember the knife glinting under the streetlight, the demand for their wallet and phone a distant echo. They complied, hands shaking, throat dry, their voice barely a whisper. 

In that moment, Amir didn't just lose their belongings; they lost something deeper-a sense of safety, a piece of their identity. After the incident, they felt as though they were drifting through life in a fog. A routine that once brought them comfort began to feel suffocating. They struggled to focus at work, their mind replaying the encounter over and over. Every patient they treated reminded them of their vulnerability, every barking dog felt like a siren announcing an impending threat. The clinic, once a sanctuary, morphed into a battleground where their anxiety loomed large.

Amir's partner, Sam, notices the change. They have been together for two years, and Sam has seen Amir's passion for their work dim. They used to come home buzzing, sharing tales of successful surgeries or heartwarming rescues. Now, the joy is replaced with silence, and their laughter is often stifled by a heavy sigh. Sam tries to reach out, asking gently, "What's going on in that beautiful mind of yours?" But Amir shrinks away from the question, caught between wanting to share and fearing the vulnerability that comes with it.

The weeks pass, and Amir finds themselves avoiding the streets at night, their schedule transforming to accommodate daylight hours. They take a longer route to work, even if it means waking up earlier. The sound of sirens sends them into a spiral, heart racing, palms sweating. They replay the scenario in their head, analyzing every detail, wishing they could go back and change the outcome. The weight of shame settles in-why didn't they fight back? Why didn't they scream? 

In therapy, Amir reveals these thoughts, their voice trembling as they recount the night of the mugging. The room feels heavy with unspoken fears as they talk about their struggles at work, how the sight of a dog in distress now triggers an overwhelming sense of helplessness. They share stories of clients who come in distraught over their pets, and how each emotional encounter feels like a mirror reflecting their own trauma. 

Yet, amid the darkness, there are glimmers of light. Amir talks about the comfort of Sam's presence, how they've created a safe space at home, filled with laughter and warmth, even when Amir is distant. They reminisce about the first time they rescued a kitten, the way it curled into their palm and purred softly, a small creature that needed protection. It's a beautiful memory, one that makes them smile, and they cling to it like a lifeline.

As the sessions progress, Amir begins to explore the idea of reclaiming their narrative, recognizing that within the fear lies a strength they never knew they had. They are learning that healing is not linear; it ebbs and flows like the tide. But for now, they continue to navigate the complexities of their emotions, one session at a time, one heartbeat at a time.

Amara is a 42-year-old divorced woman who works on an assembly line at a factory on the outskirts of a midwestern city. She came to the United States as a refugee from Central Africa nearly a decade ago, after surviving a period of detention and torture by state security forces. She was held for three weeks in a concrete room with no windows, during the rainy season, when the air was thick and damp. She was interrogated repeatedly, beaten, and subjected to electric shocks. She remembers the smell of mildew and sweat and the metallic scent of blood, a smell that still comes to her without warning. The men who held her wore heavy cologne, and one of them was named Daniel. She was released suddenly, for reasons she still does not understand, and eventually made her way to the United States.

In the years since, Amara has built a fragile life. She works long shifts, lives alone, and keeps to herself. But the past has not stayed in the past. On the factory floor, when a coworker brushes past her too closely, her body reacts before her mind has time to understand. Her shoulders lock, her breath shortens, and she feels a surge of alarm that makes no sense in the fluorescent-lit safety of the assembly line. She has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place, and that she is no longer capable of the things that once defined her-her resilience, her independence, her ability to trust her own judgment. She has also lost faith in her body. It feels like a traitor now, something that can betray her with a racing heart or a sudden shudder, and she can no longer trust it to keep her safe. These beliefs harden every time she is triggered, because each reminder of the past feels like proof that danger is still near.

Weather is a particular problem. When the sky turns gray and the rain begins, Amara's mind pulls her back into that windowless room. The memory feels unreal, as though it belongs to someone else, yet it also feels inescapable. The smell of damp concrete returns, and she finds herself scanning the factory for exits, listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering. She jumps at ordinary noises-a dropped tool, a door slamming-and her body reacts before she can tell herself she is safe. On days like this, she struggles to concentrate, and the memory intrudes so vividly that it feels like she is back there. She has learned to keep her mind occupied all the time, filling every silent moment with a song or a mental to-do list. She wears heavy makeup, partly because it makes her feel armored, and partly because she has come to believe that if she looks different, she might be harder to recognize, harder to find. She avoids wearing clothes that resemble what she wore during her detention-dark blue, simple, loose-fitting-even though she knows this is irrational.

The connection between her memories and her strategies is tight and circular. When the memory surfaces, she immediately reaches for distraction, because the alternative-letting the memory sit-feels unbearable. But the distraction itself, the constant mental busyness, also keeps the memory fragmented and strange, like a story that never gets told fully and therefore never gets integrated. The memory feels alien, as though it happened to someone else, and this only reinforces her sense that she is broken, that she cannot hold onto her own history. Hearing a name like Daniel on the factory floor-a supervisor calling out to another worker-makes her stomach drop, and she finds herself scanning the room again, her threat system fully activated. She has come to believe that these triggers are not coincidental but meaningful, signs that danger is still tracking her.

The weight of these cycles has accumulated over months and years. Amara has stopped socializing entirely. She no longer attends the small community gatherings she once enjoyed, because the physical proximity of others feels too risky. She has lost touch with the few friends she had after her divorce. At work, she has been spoken to by her supervisor about her distractibility and her tendency to startle, which has made her feel ashamed and further convinced her that she is no longer capable. What finally brought her to seek help was a morning last month when she could not leave her apartment. The rain was steady, and she was certain that if she stepped outside, something terrible would happen. She called in sick, then sat on her floor for hours, listening. She is afraid that she is losing her grip on the life she has built. She is hoping, though she does not say it easily, that someone can help her feel that the past is truly over.

Leila is a 45-year-old Middle Eastern woman who has been working as an auditor for over two decades. Her life took a dramatic turn several years ago when she was involved in a combat incident during her deployment to Iraq. The traumatic event she experienced has left lasting scars, both emotional and psychological. On that fateful day, Leila and her unit were ambushed by enemy forces in a remote desert region. The explosions rang out suddenly, and the ground shook violently as shrapnel and debris flew through the air. She remembers flashes of gunfire and the acrid smell of smoke mixed with cologne from one of her fellow soldiers who had been struck down. Leila managed to survive but the memory of that day remains fragmented and incomplete. There are parts of what happened she simply cannot recall, no matter how hard she tries. Since returning home, Leila has found herself waking up in cold sweats from nightmares, reliving those terrifying moments over and over again. The scent of a certain cologne can instantly transport her back to that traumatic event, filling her with intense fear and anxiety. Even the sound of an explosion or a loud bang triggers vivid flashbacks and overwhelming panic. Leila's coping mechanisms have become increasingly rigid and restrictive. She often thinks about how life would be different if she had never been in that combat situation, engaging in counterfactual thinking as a way to cope with her distress. Open spaces where she feels vulnerable are particularly difficult for her; she now avoids such places entirely. Instead of feeling safe outdoors, Leila is constantly scanning her surroundings, looking behind her, and planning escape routes wherever she goes. Leila's sense of safety has shrunk significantly since the traumatic event. She only feels secure in a very limited number of places, mostly within the confines of her home or familiar buildings where she works as an auditor. Even then, she constantly checks to ensure that no one is following her and meticulously plans potential escape routes before feeling comfortable. The memories of the combat incident are fragmented and disjointed. Leila feels like she is only remembering parts of what happened, with significant gaps in her recollection. This incompleteness adds to her distress, as she struggles to piece together a coherent narrative from the disconnected fragments that surface unpredictably. Leila's negative appraisals about herself have also taken root since the trauma. She believes she should have been able to protect others and feels guilty for failing to do so. Additionally, Leila has come to see the event as somehow tied to her personal character, leading her to blame herself for what happened. Her body's ongoing reactions of fear and hypervigilance further reinforce her belief that she is still in danger, even though she knows rationally that she is safe. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have strained Leila's relationships and impacted her work as an auditor. She has become increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings and professional networking events where open spaces or unfamiliar faces might trigger her anxiety. The constant need to check her surroundings and plan escape routes has also made it difficult for her to focus on her job tasks. What finally brought Leila to seek help was a particularly intense bout of nightmares followed by a debilitating panic attack at work, which forced her to take an extended leave of absence. She is most afraid that she will never truly feel safe again and that the trauma will continue to define who she is. However, she also hopes that with professional support, she can regain some sense of control over her life and learn strategies to manage her symptoms effectively. Leila's journey towards healing involves confronting these fears step-by-step, understanding the fragmented nature of her memories, and gradually expanding her safe zones while reducing avoidance behaviors. Through therapy, Leila aims to process her trauma more fully and reclaim a greater sense of security in her daily life.

Rodrigo

Rodrigo Hernández had been a parole officer for twenty-three years when the incident happened. He had built a reputation for fairness-tough but principled, the kind of officer who could sit down with a man fresh out of prison and see something worth salvaging. His colleagues respected him. His parolees, many of them, actually listened to him. He had come to believe that his job was to enforce the law while holding onto the possibility that people could change. That belief had become the architecture of his life.

On a humid afternoon in June, Rodrigo was conducting a home visit in a neighborhood where three of his cases lived. He had parked his unmarked sedan on the corner, and as he approached the apartment building, he noticed Officer Delgado-a patrol officer he had known casually for years-standing outside with his hand on his duty belt. Rodrigo raised his hand in greeting. What happened next occurred in fragments that his mind still refuses to assemble into a coherent whole. There was shouting. Someone-not Rodrigo-had a gun. Delgado moved toward Rodrigo, and then Rodrigo felt the impact, a blow to his ribs so violent it drove the air from his lungs. He fell. There was more shouting, and then Delgado was on top of him, striking his face, his shoulders, his arms as Rodrigo tried to shield himself. When it ended, Rodrigo was bleeding from a gash above his eye, his ribs screaming, and Delgado was being pulled away by other officers who had arrived. The story that emerged was a terrible mistake: Delgado had been responding to a call about an armed robbery suspect in the area. He had seen Rodrigo approaching and, in a moment of catastrophic confusion, thought he was the suspect. The department's internal investigation found that Delgado had acted recklessly but without malice. No charges were filed. Delgado was suspended for two weeks.

In the months after, Rodrigo began to notice that his body had become a stranger to him. His heart would race without warning-sometimes in his office, sometimes at home-and he would grip the edge of his desk or the kitchen counter, certain that something terrible was about to happen. He found himself unable to enter silence without dread. When his wife, Maria, would sit beside him in the evening without speaking, he would feel his shoulders tense, his breath shallow. The quiet felt pregnant with danger, as though violence itself lived in the space between words. At the office, he started scanning the hallways before he moved through them, noting exits, watching hands, tracking the position of everyone around him. His colleagues began to comment that he seemed distracted, that he had become rigid in his interactions.

The memory itself had become slippery. Rodrigo could recall the heat of that afternoon, the moment he raised his hand to greet Delgado, but when he tried to hold the rest of it in his mind-the sequence of blows, the sound of his own voice-it dissolved like something too extreme to be real. He found himself pushing it away before he could examine it fully, as though looking at it directly would shatter something essential in him. The worst part was not what he remembered but what was missing. He knew he had been beaten, but entire sections of the event had simply vanished. Sometimes he wondered if he was exaggerating it in his mind, if he had imagined some of it, because surely something that violent would leave a complete memory, not these fragmentary, unreliable pieces.

What had broken him most completely was not the violence itself but the betrayal. Delgado was a cop. Rodrigo was a cop. They inhabited the same world, followed the same code. And when the system that was supposed to hold Delgado accountable-the investigation, the department-had essentially shrugged and moved on, Rodrigo felt the ground shift beneath him. The institution that had been his home for nearly a quarter-century had failed him utterly. No charges. Two weeks' suspension. The injustice of it sat in his chest like a stone. He had spent his career believing in accountability, in consequences, in the possibility of redemption through the system. Now he understood that the system protected its own, and he was not protected.

For months, Rodrigo continued to work. He conducted his parole visits, filed his reports, sat across from men trying to rebuild their lives. But he had begun to avoid situations where he might encounter other officers. He would take longer routes to avoid the precinct. When people misbehaved-when a parolee missed an appointment, when someone cut him off in traffic-he felt a surge of rage so intense it frightened him, as though all the injustice he could not direct at the system was pouring into these smaller moments. Maria had noticed the change. She had stopped trying to sit with him in the evenings. His supervisor had asked him, carefully, if he was all right.

It was his daughter, calling from out of state, saying she was worried about how he sounded on the phone, that made Rodrigo finally admit that something was profoundly wrong. He had come to believe that he could not trust the world to be fair, that danger lurked in silence and in the hands of people he thought he knew, that his own mind could not be trusted to remember what had happened to him. He made an appointment with a therapist, sitting in the waiting room with his jaw clenched, wondering if talking about it would make it real or make it disappear entirely.

Mateo, at seventy, still finds the mornings the hardest. The quiet of his large, empty house in San Juan often feels less like peace and more like a vacuum, waiting to be filled by something jarring. He moves through his routine with a practiced efficiency - coffee, a quick scan of the local news headlines (always careful to avoid anything too graphic or political), then to his small, impeccably kept dental office on the ground floor of his home. Even after all these years, he feels a familiar tension knotting his shoulders as he unlocks the door. Each click of the lock, each creak of the floorboards, is registered, assessed. His world has become a series of low-level threat assessments.

He was fifty then, a busy man, his practice thriving. It was a Tuesday afternoon, a beautiful day, just after lunch. He'd stepped out for a moment, walking towards the Plaza de la Cultura, needing some fresh air between patients. The sun was warm on his face, the sounds of the city a familiar hum. Then, a roar. Not a car backfiring, not thunder, but a sound that seemed to tear the very fabric of the air. It was followed by a concussive blast that threw him backward, sending him sprawling on the cobblestones. Dust, smoke, the acrid smell of burning metal and something else, something organic and horrifying, filled his nostrils. He remembers the screams, the frantic scramble of people, the sight of twisted metal and shattered glass where a moment before had been a vibrant street. He saw injured people, their faces contorted in pain and shock, their clothes torn. He remembers the silence that followed the initial chaos, a deafening hush broken only by whimpers and the distant wail of sirens growing closer. He got up, his body shaking uncontrollably, and simply walked away, back towards his office, his mind a blank.

For weeks, the smell of burning or the sound of a distant siren would send him spiraling. He'd be back on the ground, the dust in his eyes, the screams in his ears. He couldn't sleep; every shadow, every unexpected noise, felt like a prelude to another disaster. His hands, usually so steady, would tremble during delicate procedures. He'd jump at the sudden whir of the drill or the suction pump, his heart hammering against his ribs. He felt a profound sense of guilt, a gnawing question of "why me?" when so many others had been hurt or worse. He tried to explain it to his wife, Elena, but the words felt inadequate, the fear too personal, too unspeakable. He started avoiding the news, avoiding conversations about the bombing, even avoiding the plaza itself. He threw himself into his work, finding a perverse comfort in the meticulous, controlled environment of his dental chair.

The years stretched on, but the shadow of that day never truly lifted. The vivid flashbacks became less frequent, but the underlying dread remained, a constant, low-frequency hum beneath the surface of his life. He became hypervigilant, always scanning exits, always aware of his surroundings, particularly in public places. Loud noises still made him flinch, his heart rate spiking. He grew increasingly irritable, snapping at Elena over trivial things, then immediately regretting it, retreating further into himself. He felt a profound sense of detachment, as if he were watching his own life from a distance. The joy he once found in his hobbies, in family gatherings, slowly dissipated. He was present, but not truly there.

Then, five years ago, Elena passed away peacefully in her sleep. His grief was immense, but it was compounded by the old, familiar numbness. He found it difficult to truly mourn, difficult to feel the depth of his loss, because a part of him had already been walled off for so long. Her absence only amplified the silence in his home, making the world feel even more precarious. He continued to work, seeing fewer patients now, the routine a lifeline, a structure in an otherwise formless existence. He still takes pride in his work, in the precise hand movements, the careful attention to detail. Yet, sometimes, while leaning over a patient, the faint smell of antiseptic can unexpectedly mingle with the phantom scent of smoke, and for a fleeting, terrifying moment, he's back on that street, the roar echoing in his ears. He quickly blinks it away, takes a slow, deep breath, and continues, his hands steady, his face impassive, carrying the weight of a moment that refuses to let go.

The rain falls on that November evening. They walk back to their apartment after an early shift at the animal hospital, keys already in hand, mind already drifting to the overdue bills on the kitchen counter. Then the shadow detaches from the alley. A voice barks something sharp. A knife catches the streetlight. Time folds. The wallet comes out. The hand comes up. Then just the sound of footsteps fading into the damp concrete. They stand there long after the danger passes, breath catching in their throat, heart hammering against their ribs like a trapped bird. The cold seeps through their jacket, but they do not move until the streetlights flicker back on, one by one, like they are checking the perimeter. In the weeks that follow, the city changes. Sidewalks become minefields. Headlights sweeping across dark streets make their palms sweat. They stop taking the shortcut past the bodega. They start sleeping with the bedroom door locked, a kitchen knife on the nightstand, and their phone charged and within arm's reach. Sleep becomes a negotiation. Every car backfiring in the garage sends them jolting upright, breathless, scanning the ceiling before realizing they are safe. Their partner, Sam, learns to speak in softer tones, to tap twice before entering the room, to never startle them when they are on the couch. They love Sam fiercely, but intimacy now feels like crossing a tightrope. They flinch at sudden touches, pull away when hands move too quickly, and wake up gasping when Sam reaches for them in the dark. They apologize, they try again, but the space between them feels charged, waiting for a spark. At the clinic, the routine once felt like a steady rhythm. Now, the ringing phones feels like a siren. When a client's dog whines too loudly, their stomach tightens. They catch themselves hesitating before reaching into an examination room, their fingers curling back like they might be grabbed. They have started double-checking the back door locks three times. They tell themselves it is just being careful, but they know it isn't. The trust they once place in the work-the familiar weight of a cat on the exam table, the predictable cadence of a well-run day-has frayed. They miss the version of themselves who could sit quietly in a waiting room and listen. Now, every interaction feels like a performance. They smile through appointments, nod at complaints, and sign charts with a hand that sometimes trembles. They wonder if the other veterinarians notice how they avoid the back alley storage room, or how they schedule their breaks for broad daylight. At twenty-six, they have always believed they are built for endurance. Now, endurance feels like bracing for a blow that never stops coming. They catch their reflection in the clinic's glass doors and see someone older, someone wound too tight. Sam asks if they want to go to the farmers market next weekend. They say yes, then immediately calculate which exits are nearest. Their Middle Eastern family calls on weekends, their mother's voice warm in Arabic, but answering the phone now requires a deep breath and a practiced calm. They do not tell them about the nights spent staring at the ceiling, or how the scent of rain still pulls them back to that alley. They worry about carrying this quietly, about becoming a burden, about losing the ground beneath them. Today, they sit across from me, hands folded tightly in their lap. The clinic's parking lot is visible through the window, a sea of parked cars that makes their shoulders rise. They describe a dream from last night where the alley stretches into a hospital corridor, the walls closing in. They speak about it without flinching, but their knee will not stop bouncing. They order tea they do not need, just to have something to do with their hands. They are still here, still showing up, still trying to hold themselves together in a world that suddenly feels like it could crack open at any moment.

Mr. Tane's Vigil

Mr. Tane has worked the evening shift at the supermarket for nearly twelve years. He knows the regulars by name, remembers which customers prefer paper over plastic, and takes pride in the efficiency of his register. At seventy-one, he's one of the older cashiers on staff, but he's reliable-the kind of employee managers don't worry about. This consistency has always been important to him, a thread running through his life since his days as a carpenter in Samoa before he and his wife migrated to Australia.

Three months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late autumn, a man came through his line. Mr. Tane was processing a customer's transaction when he heard the shout-sharp, angry, incomprehensible at first. He looked up to see another cashier, a young woman named Sophie who'd been working there only a few months, being grabbed by a man with a knife. The blade caught the fluorescent light. Mr. Tane remembers this detail with unusual clarity: how the light glinted off the metal. What happened next moved in fragments. The man demanding money. Sophie's face-the particular shape of her mouth as she cried out. The manager running toward them. The moment the blade found Sophie's shoulder, and the sound she made, and then the blood spreading across her blue uniform like spilled juice.

The police came. Sophie was taken to hospital. She recovered, though she no longer works at the supermarket. Mr. Tane gave his statement to the officers, answered their questions, and went home.

But he hasn't returned to work the same way since.

Now, when Mr. Tane sits at his register, his shoulders remain tense. His hands shake slightly as he processes transactions, though he hides this by gripping the counter. He's hyperaware of every customer who approaches, scanning them for signs of aggression he cannot quite define. Sometimes, when someone raises their voice or moves too quickly, his heart lurches into his throat. He finds himself positioning himself differently at the register, calculating angles of escape, noting where the security guards stand.

His wife notices he doesn't sleep well. He lies awake beside her, replaying the scene, sometimes jolting upright convinced he's hearing Sophie's cry again. When he does sleep, he dreams of the blade-not just what happened, but variations: the knife finding him, finding his wife, finding other people he cares about. He wakes exhausted.

The worst part is that he's begun to resent being at work. For twelve years, the supermarket was a place where he felt capable and present. Now it feels dangerous in a way he cannot articulate to his managers. He finds himself irritable with customers over minor inconveniences, then immediately guilty for his impatience. He's called in sick three times in the past month, something he's never done before. When he's home, he watches the news obsessively, noticing every report of violence, every robbery, every stabbing.

His wife has gently suggested he might talk to someone. Mr. Tane resists this idea. He's not the one who was hurt. Sophie was the victim. He was simply there. Yet he cannot shake the feeling that something fundamental shifted that Tuesday evening-that the world revealed itself to be more fragile and violent than he'd allowed himself to believe, and he cannot unknow this.

He still goes to work. He still processes transactions with practiced efficiency. But something in him remains at that register on that autumn evening, watching the blade catch the light.

Amina was a 42-year-old African American woman who had been working on a factory line for several years and was referred after describing a severe post-traumatic stress picture that had been building since her divorce and the period that followed the torture she had endured. She spoke about the event carefully, as if the details still sat just beyond what she could comfortably hold in mind. During that time she had been forced into prolonged physical proximity with the people who harmed her, unable to create distance or predict what would happen next. She described how, even now, the memory did not settle into the usual shape of something that had happened to her; it felt so extreme that she could hardly believe it was real, and at moments it seemed to belong to someone else altogether. When she tried to speak about it, she sometimes caught a smell from that time-an odor that seemed to arrive before the rest of the memory did, bringing back the same dread and making the experience feel immediate again.  

In the months after the event, Amina noticed that certain everyday things could set off a wave of fear. Being physically close to people made her tense, especially if someone stood too near in a line or came up behind her without warning. Hearing names that reminded her of those involved in the torture could make her go still for a moment, as though she had been pulled back into that setting without permission. She also became uneasy when the weather looked or felt similar to the weather at the time it happened; a certain kind of heavy heat or atmosphere could make the day feel wrong to her before anything else had occurred. At work, where she stood close to others on the factory floor and had to tolerate the constant movement of bodies and machines around her, these moments were hard to hide. She would shift away from co-workers, choose tasks that kept some space between her and others when she could, and try to keep her face controlled so no one would notice how abruptly her fear rose.  

Amina had come to rely on several ways of managing the sense that she might be pulled back into the terror at any moment. She wore heavy make-up more often than she had before, partly because it helped her feel more covered and less exposed, and partly because it gave her something deliberate to do with her appearance when she felt unsettled. She made a point of keeping her mind occupied all the time, filling silence with work, chores, or constant movement so there would be less room for images or sensations to surface. She also avoided wearing clothes that were similar to what she had worn during the traumatic period, explaining that certain fabrics, cuts, or combinations made her feel too close to that time and too aware of her own body. These habits had gradually changed how she moved through ordinary life; getting dressed for the factory each morning could become a long, tense process, and if she was late or distracted she might turn back twice to change something before leaving home.  

What frightened Amina most in daily life was how quickly her body seemed to react before she had even had time to think. She described herself as constantly listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, scanning for a door, a step, or a shift in the hallway that would tell her she was not alone. Ordinary noises-an object dropping, a sudden voice, a door closing hard-could make her jump in a way that felt disproportionate even to her. She did not experience this as a choice but as her body sounding an alarm that her mind had not yet caught up with. That sense of physical unreliability was deeply upsetting to her. She said she no longer trusted her own body, because it seemed to respond as though danger were present even when she knew, logically, that she was at home or at work and nothing overtly threatening was happening.  

Amina spoke with sadness about what she had lost in herself. Before the trauma, she had seen herself as capable and steady; now she felt no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her. The world, in her view, had become a dangerous place, and she moved through it with the expectation that harm could appear suddenly. This had changed how she related to others, and it had made her smaller in her own life. She came to treatment after a particularly difficult stretch in which these reactions had become harder to manage at work and at home, leaving her exhausted from constantly trying to stay occupied and from bracing for sounds, names, close contact, and changes in the weather. She said she wanted help because she was tired of living as if danger were always just about to enter the room, and she hoped for some way to feel safe in her body again, even if only little by little.

The Weight of Still Water

Kai is twenty-two years old, a UX designer at a small digital agency in the city, and by most outward appearances he is doing exactly what a young man his age should be doing - building a career, learning his craft, navigating his twenties. His colleagues know him as quiet and meticulous, someone who can spend hours refining the flow of a single interface until it feels effortless to the user. What they do not know is that he has not slept a full night in fourteen months.

In the spring of last year, Kai traveled back to his home province in the Philippines to visit his grandmother and extended family. He had grown up partly in that coastal town - a place of warm evenings, fishing boats, and the particular smell of salt and woodsmoke that he associated with childhood safety. He was there for three days when the typhoon made landfall. The storm surge came faster than anyone had anticipated. Kai remembers standing at the window watching the street turn into a river, and then the water was inside, and then it was at his waist, and then he was holding his grandmother's arm while she lost her footing and the current pulled her from his grip. She was recovered alive, found clinging to a neighbor's roof three streets away. He did not know this for nearly six hours.

Those six hours are where Kai lives now, even when he is sitting at his desk in an air-conditioned office in the city.

The intrusions arrive without warning or invitation. He will be reviewing a prototype - a simple onboarding screen, blue and white and completely ordinary - and the color will shift in his peripheral vision and suddenly he is back in that room, water rising, his grandmother's wrist sliding through his fingers. His heart rate spikes before his conscious mind has registered anything. He pushes back from his desk, excuses himself to the bathroom, and waits for the sensation to pass. It usually takes about ten minutes. He has become very good at finding reasons to step away.

At night, sleep is a negotiation he often loses. He keeps the television on, low volume, because silence feels like the moment just before the water came through the door. When he does sleep, he wakes from dreams that are not quite replays - sometimes the water is black, sometimes his grandmother does not come back - and he lies in the dark with his chest tight, running through what he knows to be true: she is alive, she is fine, he is in the city, he is safe. The reassurance helps, but only partially, and only for a while.

He has stopped going to the beach. This is not a small thing for someone who grew up swimming in the South China Sea. His friends invite him to weekend trips and he declines with easy excuses - a deadline, a freelance project, fatigue. He has become skilled at the architecture of avoidance, which perhaps makes sense for someone who spends his professional life designing the paths people take through spaces. He knows what it means to remove friction. He has removed every possible path that leads back toward water, toward flooding news coverage, toward the particular sound of heavy rain against glass.

What troubles him most, he says, is not the fear itself but the person the fear has made him. He describes himself before the typhoon as someone who was "open" - willing to travel, to try things, to be present with people he loved. Now he feels like he is watching his own life through a screen, always one step removed, always monitoring the edges of the frame for something that might go wrong. He worries that the person he was before the water came in is someone he cannot find his way back to, and he is not entirely sure he knows how to design a path toward that.

The incident unfolded on a rain-slicked service road behind the veterinary hospital where Samir worked the night shift. A stranger had stepped from the shadows of the ambulance bay, pressing a knife against his ribs while the engine's diesel fumes and the mugger's sour breath flooded the alley. When Samir had frozen, he had felt the cold metal and the sudden, violent violation of his personal space. That moment of terror became the anchor for everything that followed. Over the next few weeks, the assault refused to stay contained. The olfactory recall would strike without warning in the exam room when a client's cheap cologne or the antiseptic cleaner caught the breeze, instantly dragging Samir back to the alley. When trying to explain the breakdown to his partner, Samir would lose the thread entirely, hands trembling as the narrative fractured. This involuntary memory intrusion directly fed his negative appraisals; each unbidden flashback convinced him he had permanently lost his happiness and that he could no longer rely on others to keep him safe. Consequently, his constant vigilance took over. He found himself scanning every crowded street for threatening postures and checking behind him whenever footsteps echoed, even at home where he felt perpetually alert and trapped. His professional environment quickly became a minefield. During a routine surgery, a sudden drop in a medical instrument's metal tray triggered a full somatic memory of the mugger's grip. The threat system hijacked his response: instead of calling for help, Samir adopted a fawn response, becoming overly compliant and apologetic to the anesthesiologist until the panic subsided. This maladaptive strategy, combined with his growing belief that the world was fundamentally unpredictable, drove him to avoid going out entirely. He began calling in sick, rationalizing that if he stayed indoors and pretended the event hadn't been that severe, he might eventually stop feeling terrified. However, this avoidance only intensified his physiological scanning. By refusing to leave his apartment, his nervous system remained stuck in a defensive loop, making every minor noise feel like a precursor to violence. The more he tried to dismiss the trauma, the more his negative appraisals hardened, convincing him that he had to be especially careful because danger was inevitable. These beliefs, in turn, kept his memory systems hypersensitive; his mind braced for threat so constantly that it misfired, turning ordinary stimuli into full traumatic recalls. The isolation strained his relationship, and the weight of his unprocessed symptoms finally forced him into our intake office. He had come to believe that his former optimism was gone, replaced by a relentless need to monitor his surroundings for danger. What frightened him most was that his avoidance had made him a ghost in his own career, leaving him uncertain if he could ever return to treating animals or trusting his own perception of reality. He sat now, hands folded tightly in his lap, hoping for a way to untangle the memories without losing his livelihood, and dreading the thought that his hypervigilance might never quiet down.

Owen had always been drawn to service, a calling that led him first to humanitarian work in conflict zones before returning to his community to become a firefighter. It was during his time as a relief worker in a besieged city that his world irrevocably shifted. He remembered the day vividly: a routine aid convoy, winding through narrow, rubble-strewn streets, when the sudden, staccato burst of automatic gunfire erupted from an alleyway. Owen was in the lead vehicle, and the sight of armed figures emerging from the shadows, their faces obscured, had frozen him in a moment of pure terror. He'd barely managed to scramble out of the truck and seek cover, the frantic shouts of his colleagues and the desperate screams of civilians echoing in his ears. The feeling of being utterly trapped, the desperate search for an escape route, and the chilling certainty that any stranger could be a threat had seared itself into his memory.

Years later, back home in the relative safety of his American suburban life, the echoes of that day continued to shape Owen's reality. He found himself constantly on edge, a pervasive sense of vigilance clinging to him even within the familiar walls of his own home. His wife, Sarah, would sometimes find him awake in the dead of night, listening intently to the house settle, convinced he heard something amiss. He felt on guard, a sentinel in his own living room, unable to truly relax.

This hypervigilance extended far beyond his house. Whenever Owen entered a new building, whether it was the grocery store or the fire station's briefing room, his eyes immediately darted around, meticulously scanning for exits. He would instinctively position himself in restaurants or waiting rooms so that he was always close to an escape route, his back to a wall, his gaze sweeping the room. It wasn't a conscious decision at first, but over time, it became an ingrained habit, a silent, internal mandate he couldn't ignore. What frightened him most was the persistent feeling of threat from strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations. A fellow parent at his daughter's school playground, a cashier at the supermarket, or a passerby on the street - anyone who moved towards him unexpectedly would trigger an immediate spike of alarm, his body tensing, his mind racing through potential dangers, a phantom echo of those armed figures from the alleyway.

These anxieties began to cast a long shadow over his life and relationships. Owen had once enjoyed the camaraderie and physical demands of his firefighting career, but now, even simple things felt fraught. He started to avoid exercise, a crucial part of his physical readiness for the job. Going to the gym felt too exposed, too vulnerable, and running outdoors brought back the feeling of being hunted. He found himself making excuses, letting his fitness wane, much to Sarah's quiet concern.

More subtly, Owen began to push away positive emotions, a strategy he had adopted without fully understanding why. When Sarah would laugh joyfully, or when his daughter would excitedly share a drawing, a part of him would instinctively recoil from the warmth. He had come to believe, on some deeper level, that allowing himself to feel truly happy, truly content, was a dangerous indulgence. It felt like letting his guard down, making him vulnerable to the sudden, devastating loss he had witnessed in the war zone. He struggled to fully engage in moments of joy, a quiet distance growing between him and his family as he unconsciously erected barriers against anything that felt too good, too fragile.

The cumulative effect of these changes had been isolating. Sarah noticed his increasing detachment, his jumpiness, and the way he always seemed to be "on." The once vibrant man she married was now a shadow, constantly watchful, emotionally distant. The final impetus to seek help came after a particularly tense evening where a neighbor simply knocked on their door to return a borrowed tool, and Owen's disproportionate reaction - a surge of panic and a desperate urge to bolt - scared him deeply. He knew he couldn't continue living this way, perpetually bracing for a danger that never arrived, yet never truly feeling safe. He wanted to feel present again, to reconnect with his family, and to reclaim some semblance of the peace he had lost.

Keanu had worked the same checkout lane for twelve years, the rhythms of beeps and rustling plastic bags a steady, comforting beat to his days. Now, at seventy-one, the sounds were a minefield. It had been six months since the night he'd looked through his neighbor's open door. The memory wasn't a story he could tell, not even to himself. It was more like a collection of broken glass shards in his mind: the high, terrified wail of an infant, the ugly sound of a man's shouting, the sharp crack of a door slamming shut like a gunshot. He couldn't string the pieces together into a clear picture. When his wife, Leilani, had asked him what was wrong, what he had seen, the words had caught in his throat. He'd started to explain, then lost the thread completely, feeling a profound shame at his inability to make sense of it. It felt like a critical part of the memory was simply gone, leaving him with only the raw, disjointed horror.

This fragmentation followed him into his life. At work, he was in a constant state of high alert, his body tensed as if awaiting an attack. The automatic doors swishing open behind him would cause him to flinch violently, his heart hammering against his ribs. He had come to believe that danger could erupt from anywhere, at any moment. He found himself watching customers with an intensity that felt alien to him. He'd scan couples, especially those with young children, looking for a flicker of anger in their eyes or a tension in their grip. Any sudden movement-a customer reaching too quickly for their wallet, a child lunging for a candy bar-would send a jolt of pure panic through him, an instinctive reaction that screamed danger before his mind could catch up. His manager had spoken to him twice about his jumpiness, about the way he sometimes stared at people.

The most difficult trigger was the sound of a baby crying. A few weeks ago, a young mother had come through his line, her infant screaming with colic. The sound had bypassed his ears and seemed to lodge directly in his chest, a physical pressure that made it hard to breathe. He fumbled the woman's change, his hands shaking, a cold sweat breaking out on his brow. All he could see was the image from that night, a flash of something small and helpless. He felt a profound sense of discomfort settle over him in these moments, a feeling that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was powerless within it.

This powerlessness had curdled into a hard, cold anger. He was certain the man from that night had faced no consequences. He had called the police, but they had left after a few minutes, accepting the couple's story that it was just a loud argument. The system that was supposed to protect the innocent had failed. This belief had become a lens through which he saw everything. He would watch the news and feel a bitter certainty that justice was a lie, that the people responsible for terrible things were never held to account. This cynicism bled into his personal life, creating a chasm between him and Leilani. She would try to talk to him, to hold his hand, but he felt a profound emptiness, a sense that all his softer emotions had been burned away. He felt dead inside, going through the motions of his life but experiencing none of it.

Over the months, this feeling of detachment grew. He stopped going for his evening walks with Leilani, preferring to stay home where the world felt smaller and more controllable. Their conversations became shorter, strained. The silence in their small apartment grew heavier each day. It was Leilani who finally broke it. Last week, her eyes filled with tears, she told him she felt like she was living with a ghost. She missed her husband, the man who laughed at her jokes and held her while they watched television. Her words were the first thing that had truly pierced his emotional numbness in months. He is here now because he is terrified that she is right, that the man he was is gone for good. He doesn't know if he can ever feel safe again, but he holds onto a desperate hope that he can find a way to stop living inside that single, shattered moment.

Amara is a 42-year-old Eritrean-born woman who came to the United States approximately six years ago following a period of detention and torture by state security forces in her home country. She works the early shift at a packaging factory in a mid-sized Midwestern city, is divorced, and lives alone in a small apartment. She presented for psychological services after what she described as "finally running out of ways to keep going."

The events that brought Amara to this point occurred over several weeks of captivity during which she was subjected to systematic physical torture. She was held in a facility where guards announced their arrival with the sound of a heavy metal door being dragged open - a grinding, scraping noise that preceded every session. The air in the cell was thick with a particular smell she has never been able to name precisely, something chemical and damp. It was the dry season, and the heat was relentless, the kind that pressed down without relief. One of her primary interrogators shared a name with her former brother-in-law, a name she had once associated only with family gatherings. By the time she was released and eventually resettled, the architecture of her daily life had been quietly restructured around the memory of those weeks, though she did not yet understand that this was what was happening.

In the factory, Amara operates a sealing machine at the end of a conveyor line. The work requires sustained attention, which she welcomed at first - keeping her mind occupied felt like survival. She has developed an elaborate internal practice of narrating tasks to herself, counting repetitions, rehearsing shopping lists, anything to prevent her thoughts from going quiet enough for the memory to surface. But the factory presents its own difficulties. When a colleague whose name is the same as that interrogator calls out across the floor, Amara's body responds before she has registered the sound consciously - her chest tightens, her hands freeze above the machine. She has asked her shift supervisor to change her station twice without explaining why. On particularly hot summer days, when the factory floor becomes stifling and the air sits heavy and still in a way that resembles the dry season of her captivity, she has left her post mid-shift, telling no one. This has resulted in two formal warnings, and she is now at risk of losing her position.

At home, Amara keeps the television on through the night and sleeps with a chair wedged under the front door handle. She listens constantly for sounds that might mean someone is entering - a creak on the stairs, a door in another apartment. When ordinary sounds occur, a dropped pan in the hallway or a car backfiring on the street below, she startles violently, her heart already racing before any thought has formed. She had come to believe, with a quiet certainty she rarely articulated, that her body could no longer be trusted to distinguish safety from danger, that it had been rewired into something she did not recognise. She wore certain clothes in the facility, and she has not worn anything resembling them since - particular colours, particular textures. She applies heavy makeup daily, a practice that began as a way of covering bruising in the months after her release and has since become something she cannot leave the apartment without. She cannot fully explain it except to say that without it she feels exposed in a way that frightens her.

What troubles Amara perhaps most deeply is the quality of the memory itself. When she thinks about what happened, it does not feel like something that happened to her. It feels borrowed, belonging to a woman she observes from a distance, someone extreme and foreign. She has said in session that the memory is so severe she sometimes cannot believe it is real - and yet when she catches a particular smell, chemical and damp, it arrives with a physical immediacy that collapses that distance entirely. She had come to believe that she was no longer the person she was before - the woman who had worked, raised a child, managed a household - and that this incapacity was permanent. What finally brought her to seek help was her daughter, now living with Amara's sister in another state, asking over the phone why her mother never visited. Amara had no answer she could give. What she is most afraid of is that there is no version of herself left that is capable of being a mother again.

Keanu, at seventy-one, had taken the cashier job at the local market to stay busy, to have a reason to get out of the house he shared with his wife, Leilani. Now, the market felt like a minefield. The trauma was nine months ago, but for Keanu, it was a constant, looping present. He had been waiting in line at the bank to deposit a cheque when a man, agitated and shouting, had shoved his way to the front. The heavy oak door slammed shut behind another customer, the sound echoing like a gunshot in the marble hall. A young woman near Keanu, holding a baby, flinched. The baby, startled, began to wail-a piercing, terrified scream. The agitated man panicked, pulling a weapon. Keanu remembers the security guard freezing, the baby's cries, the woman's gasp, and then a confusing blur of motion before he found himself on the floor. The man was gone by the time police arrived. There was never an arrest, no justice served.

The memory of that day does not exist for Keanu as a coherent story he can tell. Instead, it lives in him as disconnected fragments: the polished gleam of the teller's counter, the specific pitch of the baby's cry, the sight of the guard's inert posture. Because these sensory fragments are so potent and intrusive, everyday sounds that echo them-a door slamming, the wail of a child-have become powerful triggers, pulling him instantly back into the fear of that moment. When he tries to explain to Leilani what is wrong, he loses the thread, the words dissolving before he can finish a sentence. This inability to form a clear narrative has become a source of profound threat; because he cannot map the event from beginning to end, he feels that danger is fundamentally unpredictable and can erupt from anywhere, at any time. The missing pieces are gaps where anything could be hiding. This fractured understanding also fuels a deep, corrosive bitterness; the gaps in his memory feel like proof of a world that doesn't make sense, a place where the people who should have protected that young woman utterly failed her.

This sense of pervasive threat now governs his life. At work, the automatic doors slide open with a soft whoosh, but if a customer lets the heavy staff door slam, Keanu flinches violently, his body reacting as if he is back on the bank's cold floor. The sound of a baby crying in the produce aisle sends a jolt of raw adrenaline through him, and he immediately begins scanning the faces of nearby shoppers, watching their hands, their movements, certain he will see the first sign of aggression. These triggers do more than just ignite fear; each one is a fresh reminder of the institutional failure that allowed the event to happen, a confirmation of his belief that the people responsible faced no consequences, leaving the world an unaccountable, dangerous place.

Over the months, these beliefs and his hypervigilance have fused into a self-sustaining loop. His conviction that the system is broken and that people are untrustworthy makes him see potential harm everywhere. He watches other people so closely for signs of danger that his manager has quietly warned him about making customers uncomfortable. This constant state of being on guard is utterly exhausting and has hollowed him out emotionally. The resulting fatigue and numbness, the feeling of being "dead inside," only reinforces his appraisal that the world is a bleak, unsafe place and that he is permanently broken by what he witnessed. He feels deadened even with Leilani, his quiet companionship replaced by a tense, watchful distance she can no longer breach.

His dark appraisals about the world's fundamental injustice seem to make the memory itself more inaccessible, as if his mind is recoiling from the full horror of what a failed system allows. These beliefs also sensitise him further to his triggers; the sound of a door slamming is no longer just a noise but the sound of an escape route being cut off in a world with no protectors. He has come to therapy at Leilani's insistence. She told him, her voice gentle but firm, that she felt she was losing him to a ghost. Keanu fears she is right. He is terrified of the vigilance leaving him, because he is certain that the moment he lets his guard down, danger will find him again. But he is even more terrified of this internal emptiness becoming permanent, of living out the rest of his years as a watchful spectre in his own life.

Sahar, a 45-year-old Middle Eastern woman and divorced auditor, has been grappling with the aftermath of her traumatic combat experience. The event left an indelible mark on her psyche, manifesting in recurring nightmares that leave her gasping for air when she wakes up from vivid scenes of explosions and gunfire. These nightmares are particularly distressing because they trigger a cascade of other symptoms. Sahar's sense of safety has been profoundly compromised since the incident. She finds herself scanning crowded streets or open spaces with an intensity that feels almost obsessive. Every bang, even a distant firecracker, sends her heart racing and compels her to check if someone is following behind her. The specific scent of cologne she encountered during the combat event now evokes intense flashbacks whenever she comes across it in public places. These triggers not only lead to heightened anxiety but also reinforce her belief that she is perpetually vulnerable. Sahar's coping mechanisms, such as constantly checking her surroundings and avoiding open spaces, are deeply rooted in these triggers. She frequently contemplates how life would have been different if the event had never occurred, a form of counterfactual thinking that adds to her distress. This tendency to think about alternatives is intertwined with her feeling that she failed to protect others during the combat situation, which is a significant negative appraisal. These negative appraisals exacerbate Sahar's feelings of vulnerability and contribute to her heightened threat perceptions. She believes that the event happened because of who she is, making it difficult for her to trust her own judgment in stressful situations. Her body's reactions-racing heart, sweating, hypervigilance-are perceived as betrayals by her own physiology, further deepening her sense of being trapped. The fragmented nature of Sahar's memories also plays a crucial role in perpetuating her anxiety and negative appraisals. There are significant gaps in her recollection of the traumatic event, and she feels like she is only remembering parts of what happened, leaving an incomplete picture that she cannot reconcile. This incompleteness fuels her suspicion and fear, as each trigger can suddenly bring back disconnected pieces of the memory, often without warning. Sahar's avoidance behaviors have seeped into her daily life as an auditor. She finds it increasingly difficult to attend meetings in open conference rooms or to travel for work-related reasons, feeling exposed and unsafe. Her tendency to identify escape routes before she feels comfortable anywhere has become a habit that limits her ability to engage fully with her professional responsibilities. The cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals is relentless. Each trigger reawakens the traumatic memories and heightens her threat perception, further reinforcing her sense of vulnerability. Her belief in her own failure compounds this, creating a self-reinforcing loop that she finds almost impossible to break free from. What finally brought Sahar to seek help was an incident where her hypervigilance led her to miss a critical detail in a financial audit report, nearly compromising her professional integrity. She is most afraid of losing control and feeling like the trauma will continue to dictate every aspect of her life. At the same time, she hopes that through therapy, she can regain some sense of normalcy and peace. Sahar's story illustrates the intricate interplay between triggers, negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, threat perceptions, and memory fragmentation, all contributing to a pervasive sense of vulnerability and fear.

Linda is a 42-year-old African woman who works as a factory worker. She has been divorced for several years and lives alone in a small apartment near her workplace. Linda's life took a dramatic turn when she was subjected to intense torture by political activists who suspected her of collaborating with the government due to her previous work in public administration before becoming a factory worker. Linda's days are marked by a profound sense of anxiety and hypervigilance, as if danger could emerge at any moment. She describes feeling constantly on edge, particularly during her commute to work, where she watches her surroundings intently for any signs of potential threats. The factory itself has become both a source of security and a place where memories of the past can resurface unexpectedly. Linda recalls one incident when the sound of machinery malfunctioning triggered flashbacks of her torture experience; the screeching noise felt like it was echoing in her ears, bringing back images she had tried so hard to suppress. In the evenings, Linda finds solace in routine activities that ground her, such as cooking dinner and watching television. However, these moments are often interrupted by intrusive thoughts about what happened to her.
